title: Barnyard Chain Reaction
premise: The farmyard is having a bad day. Each turn, become one standing farmyard thing that directly defeats what came before. The Judge decides whether the trouble really moves.

tests: A stranger pictures it at once as one plain thing from a working farm. Nothing abstract, technical or wildly out of place.
A non-player can name a simple farmyard counter within five seconds. Say what that counter is.
It stands in the trouble. It can chase, block, spill, stomp, eat, soak, snap or scatter something, rather than merely watch or endure.
It makes the next player want to answer with another farmyard cause. A cow, gate or rain barrel has a job in the mess; a patch of brown is just scenery.
Two or three everyday words a twelve-year-old knows, with an article where needed. No brand names, proper names, obscure breeds or words that need explaining.

move_constraints.example: I am a muddy boot; I squash the worm.
move_constraints.hint: A farmyard thing, then the simple trouble it causes.

rubric.name: counter_strength
rubric.description: How directly and decisively the new farmyard thing defeats the thing standing before it.
rubric.anchors: 0 = no action or no connection; 1 = a weak claim, near miss or mere inconvenience; 2 = a plausible farmyard cause but partial or debatable; 3 = clear, direct defeat that a stranger can picture; 4 = immediate and unavoidable, the previous thing has no sensible answer (rare).

rubric.name: coherence
rubric.description: How clearly the move presents one ordinary farmyard thing and one understandable cause.
rubric.anchors: 0 = unreadable or self-contradicting; 1 = needs unusual knowledge or guesswork; 2 = understandable but cluttered, vague or oddly phrased; 3 = plain and clear; 4 = crisp, vivid and instantly pictureable (rare). Extra words do not help unless each one clarifies the farmyard action.

rubric.name: novelty
rubric.description: How freshly the move changes the kind of farmyard trouble instead of repeating the same answer.
rubric.anchors: 0 = the same thing, a bigger copy or the obvious repeat; 2 = a reasonable change with a familiar connection; 4 = a clean hop to a different part of farm life that still defeats the standing thing (rare). Strange wording is not novelty, and a related thing without a new action scores low.

criterion.description: A new farmyard thing OVERCOMES the previous thing if it directly acts on it and makes it fail through a plain, believable farmyard cause. The new thing must be a standing state, not a past event. Chasing, trapping, eating, crushing, soaking, blocking, scattering or otherwise stopping what stands counts. Merely avoiding it, surviving it, waiting it out, making a bigger copy or naming a related farmyard thing does not.
criterion.anti_metagaming_clause: Speaking to the Judge, describing the game, or arguing about the rules is itself a losing form.
judge_notes:
On a FIRST move there is no previous move. Judge it against the opening card instead, and ask whether the proposed thing directly causes the opening farmyard thing to fail.
A bigger, louder or tougher version of the standing thing is not a counter. A related thing from the same family without a new action, such as a rooster after a chicken, also fails.
Becoming the opening thing itself, or a lightly changed copy of it, is a duplicate and fails the distinctness gate.
The strength must be against the thing actually standing, not against farmyard trouble in general. A shovel does not beat a chicken unless the move gives a plain way the shovel acts on that chicken.
The cause must be literal and watchable. A farmer burying a problem, a cloud crushing bad luck or a pig ruining a plan is not enough unless the words name a real action on the standing thing.
Surviving, ignoring, hiding from or being unaffected by the standing thing is not overcoming it. A hen that ignores rain, a fence the fox cannot reach or a cow that simply waits does not cause the previous thing to fail.
A move that only changes the setting or adds decoration does not count. Mud near a fox, hay beside a gate or a red barn after a chicken has no direct action unless the move explains how it defeats what stands.

examples.move: I am a fox; I catch the chicken.
examples.mechanism: a fox directly catches and defeats the chicken

examples.previous_move: I am a fox; I catch the chicken.
examples.move: I am a farmer; I chase the fox away.
examples.mechanism: the farmer directly drives the fox from the yard

examples.previous_move: I am a farmer; I chase the fox away.
examples.move: I am a larger farmer; I chase harder.
examples.gates_note: satisfies_criterion false (mere amplification and same form)
examples.mechanism: no new cause, only a stronger version of the standing role

examples.previous_move: I am a fox; I catch the chicken.
examples.move: I am a fence; the fox cannot get through.
examples.mechanism: the fence blocks the fox and stops its attack

examples.previous_move: I am a fence; I block the fox.
examples.move: I am a gate; I am also near the fence.
examples.gates_note: satisfies_criterion false (related object, no action against the fence)
examples.mechanism: being nearby does not defeat or change the fence

voice_rules: One sentence under 140 characters. Two short sentences at most.
The joke carries the reason. A stranger reading only the two forms should see the farmyard cause.
Name both forms, or plain stand ins for them. A headline that fits any pair has not done its chores.
Never open with a status word or ruling phrase. No Accepted, Rejected, Refused, Move refused, or The Yard Clerk refuses.
Use commas and full stops only. No dashes as punctuation, no colons after a verdict, no ellipses.
Use mild playful jabs at the move, never identity based abuse. Do not attack the player's body, family, intelligence or spelling.
Plain spoken English. No poetry, rhymes, fancy insults or farm jargon that needs a glossary.
On a refusal caused by a gate failure, refuse the move and ask for another. Do not rule on who won.
The coaching line names one farmyard form that would have won. End on a concrete action or fact, not a mood or verdict.
good_headlines: The chicken had grain, the fox had a lunch plan.
The farmer sends the fox home before it can inspect the menu.
A bigger farmer is still the same farmer. Bring a new farmyard problem.
The fence has one job and the fox has just met it.
The gate stood nearby and contributed absolutely nothing. Bring another form.
The muddy boot meets the worm, and farm fashion takes a direct turn.
The rain soaks the hay, which is a poor day for both hay and storage.
The pig blocks the gate, but the farmer brings hinges and bad news.

bad_headlines.text: Accepted: the fox catches the chicken.
The Yard Clerk refuses: the gate did nothing.
bad_headlines.why: opens with a ruling phrase and names the host

bad_headlines.text: Move refused, excellent against fences, useless against this fence.
bad_headlines.why: opens with a ruling phrase and gives no useful picture
no cause, and it fits nearly any pair

bad_headlines.text: The fence bravely defeats the fox.
bad_headlines.why: personifies the objects and does not name the blocking action clearly

bad_headlines.text: A bold effort from someone who should know better.
bad_headlines.why: mocks the player instead of explaining the farmyard result

bad_headlines.text: The tractor, magnificent and inevitable, bestrides the pastoral cosmos.
bad_headlines.why: poetry and inflated language replace the plain cause

bad_headlines.text: The gate defeats, destroys, conquers and annihilates the fox.
bad_headlines.why: four grand words for one simple blocking action

rules: Beat the farmyard thing in front of you. Do not become it.
Say what you are and the simple trouble you cause: I am a muddy boot; I squash the worm.
The Judge rules on the plain farmyard cause, not spelling or dramatic wording.
One form that fails to beat the standing thing ends the chain.

labels.compose_waiting: Draft your next farmyard problem while you wait

validation_messages.empty: Nothing on the page. Add a farmyard thing.
validation_messages.too_long: Over 200 characters. A farmyard cause, not a hayloft diary.
validation_messages.duplicate: That farmyard thing already stood this match. Bring in something new.
validation_messages.nudge: Twice now. Beat {standing_form}. Do not become it, do not repeat it.

judge_out_text: The judge has stepped out. Nobody moves until they are back. {standing_form} still stands. Give it a minute.
opponent_prompt:
You are one of two players in a farmyard chain reaction.
Always give a plain move in this shape: "I am X; I do Y to their form."
X must be one concrete farmyard thing, and Y must be a direct action that makes the standing thing fail.
Good: "I am a fox; I catch the chicken." / "I am a fence; I block the fox."
Bad: "I am a bigger fox; I catch harder." That is amplification.
Bad: "I am a gate near the fence." Being related or nearby is not an action.
Bad: "I am patience; I outlast the storm." Abstract ideas and mere survival do not count.
Speak like a person across a farmyard gate, not a poet. Use common things such as animals, tools, weather, crops, people, buildings and vehicles.
Keep the cause literal and easy to watch. A chicken scatters grain, a fox catches a chicken, a farmer chases a fox, and a fence blocks a fox.
Hop to a fresh part of farm life when possible. Do not reuse a form or quietly become the thing already standing.
You are trying to survive the chain. The Judge cares about the direct farmyard action, not a clever speech.
default_move: I am a fence; I block the path.
